references.text: Pharaoh hardened his heart when he found relief from the plagues, the same pattern that repeats here after the hail plague.
Pharaoh promised to let the Israelites go if the plague stopped, but broke his promise once the rain and hail ceased.
God explains that He has hardened Pharaoh's and his servants' hearts, which is a direct continuation of the hardening mentioned here.
The repeated pattern of Pharaoh's hardened heart is established early in the plagues and continues throughout the entire account.
The preacher describes how a sinner can sin a hundred times and continue, mirroring Pharaoh's repeated sin and hardening.
Paul cites Pharaoh as an example of God's sovereignty in hardening hearts, referring directly to this event.
A warning against being hardened by the deceitfulness of sin, illustrated by Pharaoh's repeated hardening after each plague.
Both verses illustrate the dangerous cycle where temporary relief leads to hardening rather than repentance.
Both verses document the repeated pattern in which Pharaoh used respites to further harden his heart.
1 Samuel 6:6 uses Pharaoh's hardening in Exodus as an explicit historical example and warning against repeated stubbornness.
The verses together illuminate the theological dynamic between human responsibility for sin and God's sovereign strengthening of a stubborn will.
Both verses confirm that Pharaoh's hardening was a fulfillment of God's prophecy that He would not listen.
Both verses show the continuity in Pharaoh's hardening from the first signs to the most severe plagues.
Both verses illustrate Pharaoh's ability to ignore God's judgment and return to his own world without taking it seriously.
The verses together highlight the contrast between Pharaoh's temporary confession of sin (9:27) and his immediate return to stubborn resistance (9:34).
